topic.title: Estimating mean and standard deviation from grouped data
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 3 is one 1-hour calculator paper of 50 marks, sat every Summer. A grouped table has opened most papers: Summer 2019, 2024 and 2026 Q1 and Summer 2022 Q3, each 2 marks for the estimated mean (M1 W1) and 3 for the estimated standard deviation (M1 W1 W1 in 2022 and 2024, MW1 W1 W1 in 2019); Summer 2022 added a 1-mark part for why the mean is only an estimate, and Summer 2024 and 2026 then changed every value by a rule. Summer 2026 used continuous classes of unequal width. The command word is Calculate, with 'an estimate of' and often 'You must show your working'.
mustMemorise: The midpoint is $\dfrac{\text{lower end} + \text{upper end}}{2}$, and it stands for every item in the class
$f x^{2}$ means $f \times x^{2}$: square the midpoint first, never square the fx entry
Divide by $\sum f$, the total frequency, not by the number of classes
Both answers are estimates because the exact values inside each class are unknown
Answers to 2 decimal places unless the question says otherwise

Histograms, frequency density and cumulative frequency curves, which belong to GCSE Mathematics
The sample standard deviation with divisor $\sum f - 1$
Unequal class widths treated by any special rule: the midpoint is used whatever the width

note.title: Mean and standard deviation from a grouped table
note.subject: further-maths

given: Mean = sum of fx over sum of f
Standard deviation = square root of (sum of f x squared over sum of f, minus the mean squared)
Addition rule, conditional probability and Spearman's coefficient (elsewhere on the same sheet)
Normal Probability Table on page 3 of the booklet
mustKnow: The midpoint of a class is the average of its two ends, and it is the x the formula uses
f x squared means the frequency times the square of the midpoint
The divisor is the total frequency, not the number of classes
Both answers are estimates because the individual values are unknown

notOnThisSpec: Median, modal class and interquartile range from a grouped table, which the Teacher Guidance says will not be asked
Histograms, frequency density and cumulative frequency curves, which belong to GCSE Mathematics
The sample standard deviation with divisor $\sum f - 1$
Unequal class widths treated by any special rule: the midpoint is used whatever the width

mustBeAbleTo: Write the midpoint of a discrete class such as 20 to 24 and of a continuous class such as 5 to under 10
Build the $fx$ column and total it
Divide $\sum fx$ by $\sum f$ for the estimated mean, keeping it unrounded
Build the $f x^{2}$ column by squaring the midpoint before multiplying by the frequency
Substitute into $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum fx^{2}}{\sum f} - \bar{x}^{2}}$ and finish with the square root
Explain in one sentence why both answers are estimates
Round to 2 decimal places and keep the data's units
sheet.howExamined: Unit 3 is one 1-hour calculator paper of 50 marks, sat every Summer. A grouped table has opened most papers: Summer 2019, 2024 and 2026 Q1 and Summer 2022 Q3, each 2 marks for the estimated mean (M1 W1) and 3 for the estimated standard deviation (M1 W1 W1 in 2022 and 2024, MW1 W1 W1 in 2019); Summer 2022 added a 1-mark part for why the mean is only an estimate, and Summer 2024 and 2026 then changed every value by a rule. Summer 2026 used continuous classes of unequal width. The command word is Calculate, with 'an estimate of' and often 'You must show your working'.
traps: Squaring the fx column instead of computing $f \times x^{2}$ (Summer 2024 Q1, Summer 2019 Q1)
Squaring the total of the fx column (Summer 2022 Q3)
Dividing by the number of classes rather than by the total frequency: rare, but named by the Summer 2019 Q1 and Summer 2022 Q3 reports as a major method error
Using a class limit or the class width in place of the midpoint
Explaining the estimate by rounding or by sample size instead of by the unknown individual values
Giving the variance where the standard deviation was asked for

noteBlocks.lede: A table that groups its data keeps the count in each class and throws the separate values away. You can still find a mean and a standard deviation from it: let the middle of each class stand for every value in it, and both answers become careful estimates.
can: Write the midpoint of a class, whole numbers or continuous
Build the $fx$ and $f x^{2}$ columns and total them
Estimate the mean and standard deviation, and say why they are estimates

noteBlocks.text: One value stands for a whole class

noteBlocks.md: Forty pupils timed their journeys to school, to the nearest minute, and the table records only which class each journey falls in. Nobody can say where inside a class a journey sits, so the value in the middle of the class stands for every journey in it. That one assumption is why every answer from a grouped table is an estimate.

noteBlocks.caption: Each dot is the midpoint that stands for every journey in its class.

noteBlocks.stem: Find the midpoints of the journey classes 1 to 5, 6 to 10 and 11 to 15 minutes.

steps.decision: Add the two ends of the class and halve: the value in its middle.
The same for the next class.
Equal classes give midpoints that step on by the class width, here 5 each time.

noteBlocks.prompt: In a grouped table of whole-number ages, one class is 19 to 25 years. What is the midpoint of that class?
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of See it, add the two ends of the class and halve: $\dfrac{19 + 25}{2} = 22$. That value then stands for everyone in the class.

twin.prompt: A class in a grouped table of marks is 35 to 41. What is its midpoint?

noteBlocks.text: Continuous classes, and classes of unequal width

noteBlocks.md: Measurements such as mass or time are often grouped as $1.0 \leqslant m < 1.5$: from 1.0 up to, but not including, 1.5. The midpoint is still halfway between the two boundaries. Classes need not be the same width, and when they differ the midpoints no longer step on evenly, so work each one out on its own.

noteBlocks.stem: Find the midpoints of the classes $1.0 \leqslant m < 1.5$, $1.5 \leqslant m < 2.5$ and $2.5 \leqslant m < 4.0$ kilograms.

steps.decision: Halfway between the boundaries of the first class.
Halfway between this class's own boundaries, whatever its width.
Each midpoint comes from its own class's boundaries, never by adding a fixed step to the one before.

noteBlocks.prompt: One class in a table of journey times is $4.0 \leqslant t < 7.0$ minutes. What is its midpoint?
noteBlocks.explain: As in See it, take the value halfway between the boundaries: $\dfrac{4.0 + 7.0}{2} = 5.5$. The width of this class, 3 minutes, does not change how the midpoint is found.

twin.prompt: A class of distances is $14 \leqslant d < 18$ kilometres. What is its midpoint?

noteBlocks.text: The mean: $\sum fx$ shared over $\sum f$

noteBlocks.md: Multiply each frequency by its midpoint: $fx$ estimates the total of the values in that class, and $\sum fx$ estimates the total of them all. Share that total over every value, $\sum f$, for the estimated mean $\bar{x} = \dfrac{\sum fx}{\sum f}$. Divide by the number of values, never by the number of classes.

noteBlocks.stem: Estimate the mean journey time from the table of 40 journeys.

steps.decision: Frequency times midpoint, row by row: each row's estimated total.
Add the column: an estimate of all 40 journeys put together.
Divide by $\sum f = 40$, the number of journeys, not by the 5 classes.

noteBlocks.prompt: A grouped table has $\sum fx = 1386$ and $\sum f = 60$ in 6 classes. What is the estimated mean?
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 3 of See it, share the total over every value: $\dfrac{1386}{60} = 23.1$. Dividing by the 6 classes would give 231, far outside any class.

twin.prompt: A grouped table has $\sum fx = 1092$ and $\sum f = 52$ in 4 classes. What is the estimated mean?
twin.explain: Divide by the number of values: $\dfrac{1092}{52} = 21$.

noteBlocks.text: The $f x^{2}$ column: square the midpoint first

noteBlocks.md: The standard deviation needs one more column, $f x^{2}$: square the midpoint, then multiply by the frequency. It is not the $fx$ entry squared. Squaring $fx$ squares the frequency as well, and the numbers balloon.

noteBlocks.title: Why the square sits on the x alone
noteBlocks.md: Each of the $f$ values in a class is taken to be the midpoint $x$, so the class adds $f$ squares of $x$: that is $f \times x^{2}$. Squaring $fx$ would count each value $f$ times over, which no data ever did.

noteBlocks.stem: Build the $f x^{2}$ column for the 40 journeys.

steps.decision: Square the midpoint first, then multiply by the frequency.
The same for each row: for 11 to 15, $15 \times 13^{2} = 2535$, never $195^{2}$.
Add the column: this total goes into the formula next.

noteBlocks.prompt: A class has frequency 9 and midpoint 14. What is its $f x^{2}$ entry?
noteBlocks.explain: As in step 1 of See it, square the midpoint, then multiply: $9 \times 14^{2} = 9 \times 196 = 1764$. Squaring the $fx$ entry, $126^{2}$, would give 15876.

twin.prompt: A class has frequency 7 and midpoint 16. What is its $f x^{2}$ entry?

noteBlocks.md: Page 2 of the Unit 3 booklet prints $\sigma = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum fx^{2}}{\sum f} - \bar{x}^{2}}$, and a grouped table is exactly what it was written for. Substitute the two totals and the unrounded mean, then take the square root last.

noteBlocks.stem: Estimate the standard deviation of the 40 journeys: $\sum f = 40$, $\sum fx^{2} = 7130$ and $\bar{x} = 12.25$.

steps.decision: Substitute into the sheet's formula, with the mean exactly as found.
The value under the root is the variance; it can never be negative.
Take the root last, to 2 decimal places.

noteBlocks.title: OCR MEI Statistics 1 2.05 Mean and Standard Deviation from Grouped Frequency and Identifying Outliers
noteBlocks.why: The same columns built one row at a time on another table; its closing part, on outliers, goes beyond this specification.

noteBlocks.prompt: A grouped table has $\sum f = 25$, $\sum fx = 425$ and $\sum fx^{2} = 7650$. What is the estimated standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?
noteBlocks.explain: As in See it, the mean first, $\dfrac{425}{25} = 17$; then $\dfrac{7650}{25} - 17^{2} = 306 - 289 = 17$, the variance, and $\sqrt{17} = 4.12$.

twin.prompt: A grouped table has $\sum f = 20$, $\sum fx = 260$ and $\sum fx^{2} = 3600$. What is the estimated standard deviation, to 2 decimal places?

noteBlocks.text: Saying why the answers are estimates

noteBlocks.md: One part of a grouped question can ask why the mean is only an estimate, for one mark. The sentence has to name what is unknown and what was used instead: the exact values inside each class are not known, so each class is represented by its midpoint. Rounding, or the size of the sample, is not the reason.

noteBlocks.stem: Say why the mean journey time of 12.25 minutes is only an estimate.

steps.working: Unknown: each pupil's exact journey time
steps.decision: The table keeps only the class each journey falls in.

steps.working: Used instead: the class midpoint, 13 for 11 to 15
steps.decision: Every journey in a class is treated as sitting at its middle.

steps.working: The exact times in each class are not known, so each class is represented by its midpoint.
steps.decision: One sentence naming both earns the mark.
It names neither the missing values nor the midpoint, so it earns nothing.

noteBlocks.prompt: Asked why a mean from a grouped table of plant heights is only an estimate, Kofi wrote: 'Because the heights were rounded to the nearest centimetre.' Does his sentence earn the mark?
options: No: it does not say the exact heights are unknown and replaced by midpoints
Yes: rounding is the reason the answer is an estimate
Yes: any sentence that uses the word estimate earns it
noteBlocks.answer: No: it does not say the exact heights are unknown and replaced by midpoints
noteBlocks.explain: As in steps 3 and 4 of See it, the mark needs what is unknown and what stood in for it: the exact heights in each class, replaced by the midpoint. Rounding names neither, so Kofi's sentence earns nothing.

twin.prompt: Asked the same about a grouped table of reaction times, Mia wrote: 'The exact times in each class are not known, so the midpoints are used instead.' Does her sentence earn the mark?
options: Yes: it names the unknown values and the midpoints that replace them
No: it must also say the times were rounded
No: it must give the mean as well
twin.answer: Yes: it names the unknown values and the midpoints that replace them
twin.explain: It says what is unknown and what stood in for it, which is the whole mark.

optionNotes.option: No: it must also say the times were rounded
optionNotes.why: Rounding is not the reason, so it adds nothing to the mark.

optionNotes.option: No: it must give the mean as well
optionNotes.why: The part asks only for the reason; the mean was found in the part before.

optionNotes.option: Yes: rounding is the reason the answer is an estimate
optionNotes.why: Rounding is a real thing, but the table would still give an exact mean if it listed every height; the grouping is what loses the values.

optionNotes.option: Yes: any sentence that uses the word estimate earns it
optionNotes.why: The mark is for the reason, not the word: it needs the unknown values and the midpoint named.

noteBlocks.md:
Write the midpoint of a class of whole numbers or of a continuous class, even when the widths differ.
Build the $fx$ column and divide $\sum fx$ by $\sum f$ for the estimated mean.
Build the $f x^{2}$ column by squaring the midpoint before multiplying by the frequency.
Substitute into the sheet's formula with the exact mean and finish with the root.
Say in one sentence why both answers are estimates.

A grouped table appears in most Unit 3 papers (Q1 in Summer 2019, 2024 and 2026; Q3 in Summer 2022): two marks for the estimated mean, three for the standard deviation, and in 2022 one for why it is an estimate. The first mark is the fx column. Stuck: write the midpoints, then the fx and f x squared columns, before anything else.

workedExamples.stem:
A courier weighed 60 parcels and grouped the masses as shown in the table.
Calculate an estimate of the mean mass, and an estimate of the standard deviation of the masses.

data.caption: Masses of 60 parcels, in kilograms; the last class is twice as wide as the others

steps.decision: Halfway between each pair of boundaries. The last class is 4 kg wide, so its midpoint is 8, not 7.
Frequency times midpoint in each row, then add the column.
Divide by $\sum f = 60$, the number of parcels. Keep the unrounded value for the next line.
Square each midpoint, then multiply by its frequency, then add.

whyMenu.explain: The square sits on the midpoint alone: 8 squared is 64, and 12 parcels of it make 768. Squaring the fx entry would square the frequency too.

steps.decision: Substitute into the sheet's formula with the unrounded mean. The value under the root is the variance.
Take the root last and give it to 2 decimal places.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: An estimated mean of $4.43$ kg and an estimated standard deviation of $2.24$ kg

twin.stem:
A librarian asked 50 pupils how many books they had read in a year and grouped the answers as 0 to 4, 5 to 9, 10 to 14, 15 to 19 and 20 to 24, with frequencies 6, 13, 17, 9 and 5.
Calculate an estimate of the standard deviation of the numbers of books.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on something you already know. What is the midpoint of the class 7 to 9?
items.skill: Midpoint of a class (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: That is the bottom end of the class. The midpoint is the value halfway along it.
That is the top of the class. Add the two ends and halve them.

items.stem: Before the lesson: in a frequency table, what does the frequency column tell you?
items.skill: Reading a frequency table (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.text: How many items fall in that class
options.feedback: Yes, and adding that column gives the total number of items, which is what you divide by.

options.text: The size of the items in that class
options.feedback: Size is in the class column. The frequency counts how many items are there.
Width comes from the two ends of the class. Frequency is a count.

items.stem: Before the lesson, and you are not meant to know this yet: a table gives classes rather than individual measurements. What is lost?
items.skill: Why grouped answers are estimates (new here, so a guess is fine)

options.text: The individual values, so every answer becomes an estimate
options.feedback: Exactly the reason examiners want in words, and the reason the midpoint is used at all.

options.text: Nothing: the class tells you each value
options.feedback: A class of 20 to 24 could hold any of those values. That is what makes the answer an estimate.
The total survives: it is the frequency column added up. What is lost is the individual values.

items.stem: A class has frequency $18$ and midpoint $32$. What is its $f x^{2}$ entry?
items.skill: Building the f x squared column

options.feedback: Yes: $18 \times 32^{2} = 18432$. Square the midpoint, then multiply.
That is the fx entry squared, $\left(576\right)^{2}$. The square belongs on the midpoint alone.
That is the fx entry with no squaring at all. The second column needs the midpoint squared first.

items.stem: A grouped table has 6 classes and $\sum f = 45$. What do you divide $\sum fx$ by for the estimated mean?
items.skill: Dividing by the total frequency, not the number of classes

options.feedback: Yes. The mean shares the total over every value, and there are 45 of them.
That is the number of classes. The reports name dividing by it as a major method error, though few made it.
That is $\sum f - 1$, the calculator's $s_{x}$ divisor. The sheet divides by $\sum f$.

items.stem: Which sentence earns the mark for why a grouped mean is only an estimate?

options.text: The exact values in each class are unknown, so the midpoint stands for them all
options.feedback: Yes. It names what is missing and what replaced it, which is the whole mark.

options.text: Because the numbers have been rounded
options.feedback: Rounding is a different idea, and the mark is not there. Say that the individual values are unknown.

options.text: Because a mean is always approximate
options.feedback: A mean of raw values is exact. It is the grouping that makes this one an estimate.

items.stem: For a grouped set, $\dfrac{\sum fx^{2}}{\sum f} = 230.5$ and $\bar{x} = 14.5$. What is the estimated standard deviation?
items.skill: Subtracting the mean squared, then rooting

options.feedback: That is the variance, the number under the root. One more step finishes it.
The mean squared was never taken off, so that is about the size of a value rather than the spread.

items.stem: In a table of continuous data the class is 5 to under 10 minutes. Which value goes in the $x$ column?

options.feedback: Yes: halfway between 5 and 10.
That is the lower end. Using it drags every estimate down.
That is the upper end, and a time of exactly that would belong to the next class. Take the value halfway along instead.

parts.stem:
A grower measured the heights, to the nearest centimetre, of 50 tomato plants.
Calculate an estimate of the mean plant height.
You must show your working.
hints: Write the midpoint of each class beside it.
$\sum fx = 1585$, and $\sum f = 50$.

commonErrors.feedback: $\sum fx$ was divided by the number of classes. Divide by $\sum f = 50$, the number of plants, and the estimate is 31.7 cm.
The bottom of each class was used instead of its midpoint, so every estimate is 2 cm light. The midpoints are 22, 27, 32, 37 and 42.

parts.stem: Explain why your answer to part (a) is only an estimate.

accepted: The exact values inside each class are not known, so the midpoint is used to stand for every value in the class.
The table only gives classes, so the exact values are not known and midpoints are used instead.

scheme.for: the individual heights inside each class are unknown, so the midpoint represents them all

hints: What does the table leave out?
Name what you used in place of the real heights.
parts.workedSolution: The table records only which class each plant is in, not its height, so every plant in a class is treated as being at the midpoint and the mean that follows is an estimate.

commonErrors.feedback: Rounding is not the reason. The individual heights are never recorded, so each class is represented by its midpoint, and that is what makes the answer an estimate.

parts.stem:
Calculate an estimate of the standard deviation for these plant heights.
You must show your working.

scheme.for: $\sqrt{\dfrac{\sum fx^{2}}{\sum f} - \bar{x}^{2}}$ with the candidate's values

hints: Square the midpoint, then multiply by the frequency: $6 \times 22^{2} = 2904$.

commonErrors.feedback: The fx column has been squared entry by entry. The substitution earns its method mark, but the column the formula wants is $f \times x^{2}$: square the midpoint first, and the estimate is 5.69 cm.
The fx column was totalled and the total squared, so $\left(\sum fx\right)^{2}$ went into the formula in place of $\sum fx^{2} = 51865$. The substitution earns its method mark; the column does not.
That is the variance. The substitution and $\sum fx^{2}$ are right; the last mark is for the root, $\sqrt{32.41} = 5.69$ cm.
The mean squared was never taken off, so the formula on the sheet was not used and what is left is the size of a height, not its spread. Subtract 1004.89 from 1037.3 first.

findTheMistake.stem: Rory was asked for an estimate of the standard deviation of the goals scored in 30 matches, grouped as 0 to 2, 3 to 5, 6 to 8 and 9 to 11 with frequencies 5, 12, 9 and 4. His working:
studentWorking: sd = square root of (7898 over 30 minus 5.2 squared) = 15.37
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 3 squares each entry of the fx column. The column the formula needs is $f \times x^{2}$: square the midpoint, then multiply by the frequency, which gives 5, 192, 441 and 400.
correction: sd = square root of (1038 over 30 minus 5.2 squared) = 2.75
findTheMistake.feedback: The midpoints and the mean are right, so both marks for the mean are safe. Line 3 squares the frequency along with the midpoint, and every line after it inherits that. Build the $f x^{2}$ column from the midpoint, and the estimate is 2.75.
